Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 64
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Jeweler
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Shouting: Shouting, Male Presence: Being alone with men, Conflict: Confrontations
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
  Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture

Vignette:
Carlos is a sixty-four-year-old jeweler who works alone in a small storefront in a mixed-use neighborhood of Los Angeles. What finally brought him to therapy was a moment he could no longer push aside: two weeks ago, a customer raised his voice over a repair estimate, and Carlos felt his chest lock, his vision narrow, and his hand drift toward the drawer where he kept a small brass hammer. He didn't touch it, but the fact that he had even considered it terrified him. The customer left, and Carlos spent the rest of the day checking his own thoughts—*am I losing control? am I becoming dangerous?*—until he drove home numb. That night, he could not stop seeing a single image: the kitchen table of his childhood apartment, splintered wood, his mother's hand flat on the surface, his father's shadow.

The trauma Carlos carries is not a war or a crime scene but a series of frozen moments from the age of seven. He remembers his father shouting, then a crash, then his mother's voice pleading, then silence. What stays with him most vividly is not the violence itself but a single frame: his mother afterward, sitting on the floor, and Carlos standing in the doorway, unable to move. He remembers thinking, *I should have stopped it.* That guilt has never loosened its hold. He can recall that kitchen scene in photographic detail—the pattern on the linoleum, the way the light fell through the blinds, the smell of burned coffee—but it exists as a handful of disconnected snapshots, not a continuous story.

For decades, Carlos built a life around not thinking about that moment. He learned to work with his hands, to focus on the tiny mechanisms of watch movements and the precise setting of stones. As a jeweler, he had to be still and calm, yet he found that relaxation itself felt dangerous. If he let his attention drift, even for a second, he worried that something terrible would happen or that his own mind would slip. So he stayed in a state of quiet vigilance, monitoring every thought that passed through his head for signs that he might be going crazy. Whenever images of that childhood kitchen surfaced, he forced them down, tried to cut them off before they could take shape.

His occupation became both a sanctuary and a trap. Alone in his shop, he could control his environment—no loud voices, no unexpected confrontations. But customers occasionally argued about prices, and when they did, Carlos would freeze, then overcompensate by agreeing too quickly, offering discounts he could not afford, just to end the exchange. He also found himself watching male customers with particular care, scanning their hands, their posture, looking for any hint of aggression. He noticed weapons or dangerous objects everywhere: a screwdriver on his bench could become a threat; a heavy paperweight; a customer's belt buckle. When others told him he was safe—that his shop was secure, that this was a quiet neighborhood—he could not make himself believe it.

Over time, Carlos's marriage faltered. His wife complained that he was unreachable, that he never relaxed, that he would flinch if she raised her voice even in excitement. He could not explain why he needed to sit with his back to the wall, why he tracked every movement in a room, why he felt a crushing sense of failure whenever he thought about his role as a husband or a father. His divorce two years ago solidified that appraisal: he had failed in his most important role in life. He saw himself as a weak man, someone who could not protect anyone, who could not even protect himself from his own memories. His connection to his community and his culture—the large family gatherings, the celebratory shouting at holidays, the easy camaraderie among men—felt lost. He stopped attending events. The noise, the proximity, the possibility of conflict made it unbearable.

Now, in his small shop, Carlos works longer hours than necessary. He avoids relaxing even at home. He is afraid of what might surface if he stops monitoring. The intrusion of that single image of his mother's hand on the linoleum has become more frequent, and the guilt that follows is so sharp that he sometimes puts down his loupe and simply stares at the wall. He came to therapy because he heard himself thinking, *I can't keep doing this alone,* and that thought felt like both a confession of weakness and the only honest thing he had said in years. He is afraid of being diagnosed as crazy, afraid of being told that he is beyond help. But beneath that fear is a quieter hope: that maybe he can learn to sit still without watching for danger, that maybe he can stop seeing that kitchen every time a voice rises in anger.
